summary:
The RIDGE Crew Health Monitor is a web based prototyping tool that allows astronauts to collect data about their health. This includes logging observations, tracking trends in vital signs, sleep and mood and exploring different body systems using an interactive body map. It shows the differences against the user's individual baselines, whilst also showing any changes to cabin conditions and radiation.

The tool was designed based on NASA's 5 hazards of human spaceflight. This provides astronauts with a greater understanding of how their health is changing as it provides both health and environmental data. It also demonstrates how a summary of health can be sent to the ground medical team to be reviewed at a later date.

This project aims to give crew members a greater understanding of how their health is changing and provides a greater amount of information to the ground medical team. This tool is a prototype and is not a diagnostic tool. More testing is required to determine how reliable, easy to use and safe it is clinically.
details:
The RIDGE Crew Health Monitor is a browser based prototype which aims to allow astronauts and medical officers to easily view health data in a space environment. This allows for the user to view health indicators, self-reported information and mission details.

The prototype was split into the 5 major hazards of human spaceflight (Radiation, Isolation and Confinement, Distance from Earth, Gravity Fields, Hostile/Closed Environments) as part of the RIDGE framework. This combines physiological data like blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, sleep and mood to create a picture of their health trends and mission details. It provides a more accurate insight of how their health is changing over time relative to their baseline values rather than standard medical advice.

The data entry section includes sections to input measurements, self-reported information, tools used, annotations and visibility to the user. Specific data types are separated such as bodily fluids and scan imaging, these are recorded as events. There is an interactive 3D model of the body which allows users to view different parts of the body and different layers (muscles, organs, nervous system etc.) to visualise bodily systems.

The Context & Exposure section includes information regarding the environment of the habitat. This includes data about the cabin such as CO2 levels, pressure, temperature, noise, light, microbial levels, radiation exposure and communication latency times. The amount of radiation is separated from any damage this may cause to the user. This project has a list of tools which include what data they collect, units, what hazard they relate to and references to research.

During the development of the project, we used a browser based prototype with charts to view health data, forms to input data and a 3D model of the body. The science behind the project uses the NASA Human Research Program. This includes the 5 hazards, current research (CIPHER) and information from the Canadian Space Agency on neutron radiation monitoring. This helps to structure information but does not provide specific medical advice.

RIDGE combines information. Users can view health trends, explore the relevant anatomy and environmental factors. The prototype also includes regular checklists and reminders to ensure regular logging. It does not make any claims about how effective it will be medically.

As a team we considered factors such as communication latency, availability of the tool on the spacecraft, confidentiality, using personal baselines, ensuring data is complete and ensuring information is clearly communicated. The prototype allows for a summary of health which can be reviewed later by the ground team. However, only a simulation of sending data to the ground has been carried out. A main aim was to have a tool that can be used mainly on the spacecraft however we need to test how reliable it is when offline and how it stores the records.

The aim is to improve clarity when reviewing health data and improve information sharing between the crew and medical. As this is still a concept and prototype it will not act as a diagnostic tool or medically approved. The readings are just examples and usability and safety for medical purposes needs to be tested.
